papers.title: 2019 Index IEEE Transactions on Affective Computing Vol. 10
papers.abstract: his index covers all technical items—papers, correspondence, reviews, etc.— that appeared in this periodical during 2019, and items from previous years that were commented upon or corrected in 2019. Departments and other items may also be covered if they have been judged to have archival value. The Author Index contains the primary entry for each item, listed under the first author’s name. The primary entry includes the coauthors’ names, the title of the paper or other item, and its location, specified by the publication abbreviation, year, month, and inclusive pagination. The Subject Index contains entries describing the item under all appropriate subject headings, plus the first author’s name, the publication abbreviation, month, and year, and inclusive pages. Note that the item title is found only under the primary entry in the Author Index.

papers.title: Transactions on Affective Computing - Celebrating the 10th Year of Publication
papers.abstract: SINCE its inception in 2010, the IEEE Transactions of Affective Computing (T-AC) has evolved in an impressive manner to become the leading journal of Affective Computing Research. This year, we are celebrating the 10thAnniversary of the IEEE Transactions of Affective Computing. In the past ten years, T-AC have not only achieved high visibility among professional working in the area of Affective Computing, but also attracted interest of neighboring communities. Going beyond pure rational behaviors, the area of Affective Computing presents exciting challenges to the field of Artificial Intelligence—in particular when focusing on spontaneous behaviors with high intraand inter-individual variability. Work on the automatic detection and interpretation of socio-emotive signals pave the way towards more natural and intuitive means of communication between humans and social robots. Principles and techniques from Affective Computing provide a solid basis for assessing user experience in the area of Human-Computer Interaction. Most importantly, our journal plays a vital role in informing about what Affective Computing research can do and what it cannot do in order to avoid misconceptions about or even misuse of technologies developed in our field. To this end, the journal includes excellent surveys covering topics as varied as automated facial expression analysis, expressive body gesture recognition, sentiment analysis or emotion recognition using EEG signals. The growing impact of T-AC is well reflected by the number of submissions which has risen again from 440 in 2018 to 526 in 2019. To deal with the higher workload, we have extended the editorial board to 33 colleagues. It is with great pleasure to announce that we couldwin 23 new highly esteemed colleagues for the editorial board of T-AC: Nadia Berthouze (University College London, UK), Joost Broekens (Leiden University, The Netherlands), Ginevra Castellano (Uppsala University, Sweden), Mohamed Chetouani (Universit e Pierre et Marie Curie, France), Chloe Clavel (T el ecom ParisTech, France),Mehdi Dastani (Utrecht University, The Netherlands), CelsoM. deMelo (US Army Research Lab, USA), Abinav Dhall (Monash University, Australia), Corina Roxana Girju (University of Illinois, USA), Guodong Guo (West Virgina University, USA), Dirk Heylen (University of Twente, The Netherlands), Jesse Hoey (University of Waterloo, Canada), Leong Hong-VA (The Hong Kong Polytechnic University, China), Mohammed H. Mahoor (University of Denver, USA), Gary McKeown (Queens University Belfast, UK), EmilyMower Provost (University ofMichigan, USA), Fabien Ringeval (Universit e Grenoble Alpes, France), Enzo Pasquale Scilingo (University of Pisa, Italy), Carlos Strapparava (Fondazione Bruno Kessler, Italy), Khiet Truong (University of Twente, The Netherlands), Alessandro Vinciarelli (University of Glasgow, UK), Shangfei Wang (University of Science and Technology of China, China), Dan Zhang (TsinghuaUniversity, China). They excellently complement the expertise of our longer-running Associate Editors: Julien Epps (The University of New South Wales, Australia), Roland Goecke (University of Canberra, Australia), Bin Hu (Lanzhou University, China), Florian Metze (CarnegieMellonUniversity, USA), Albert Ali Salah (Utrecht University, TheNetherlands), Stefan Scherer (University of Southern California, USA),Mohammad Soleymani (Institute for Creative Technologies, USA), Friedhelm Schwenker (University of Ulm, Germany), Michel Valstar (University of Nottingham, UK) and Wenming Zheng (Southeast University, China). The term of the following highly dedicated colleagues has come to an end: Ehsan Hoque (Rochester University, USA), Grace Ngai (Hong Kong Polytechnic University, China), Fabrizio Sebastiani (ISTI-CNR, Italy), Yi-Hsuan Yang (Academica Sinica, Taiwan), and Stefanos Zafeiriou (Imperial College London, UK). At this occasion, I would like to thank all our previous and current Associate Editors for their excellent services. Furthermore, I ammost grateful to the reviewers for their enormous effort they put into highest quality reviews over the years. Wonderful news is the recent Impact Factor of our journal. According to the Journal Citations Report by Clarivate Analytics, the official latest 2018 Impact Factor (IF) has risen (again) to 6.288. Likewise, the journal ranks number 29 out of 161 IEEE journals in the 2018 Journal Citation Report (JCR) by 5-year IF, and number 13 out of 133 for Computer Science— Artificial Intelligence in the 2018 JCR, and number 2 out of 23 for Computer Science—Cybernetics by the samemeasure. Another reason for joy and excitement are the T-AC Best Paper Award and the T-AC Most Influential Paper Award. The winners were selected from 88 eligible papers that have been published in T-AC Volume 8, Number 3 (July – Sept. 2017) and T-AC Volume 10, Number 2 (Jan. March 2019). papers.title: A Wide Evaluation of ChatGPT on Affective Computing Tasks
papers.abstract: With the rise of foundation models, a new artificial intelligence paradigm has emerged, by simply using general purpose foundation models with prompting to solve problems instead of training a separate machine learning model for each problem. Such models have been shown to have emergent properties of solving problems that they were not initially trained on. The studies for the effectiveness of such models are still quite limited. In this work, we widely study the capabilities of the ChatGPT models, namely GPT-4 and GPT-3.5, on 13 affective computing problems, namely aspect extraction, aspect polarity classification, opinion extraction, sentiment analysis, sentiment intensity ranking, emotions intensity ranking, suicide tendency detection, toxicity detection, well-being assessment, engagement measurement, personality assessment, sarcasm detection, and subjectivity detection. We introduce a framework to evaluate the ChatGPT models on regression-based problems, such as intensity ranking problems, by modelling them as pairwise ranking classification. We compare ChatGPT against more traditional NLP methods, such as end-to-end recurrent neural networks and transformers. The results demonstrate the emergent abilities of the ChatGPT models on a wide range of affective computing problems, where GPT-3.5 and especially GPT-4 have shown strong performance on many problems, particularly the ones related to sentiment, emotions, or toxicity. The ChatGPT models fell short for problems with implicit signals, such as engagement measurement and subjectivity detection.
